title: The Gold Coins and the Judge (ಕನ್ನಡ)
summary: A dishonest Qazi steals gold coins entrusted to him by a traveling pilgrim. Birbal uses fresh wax and olive oil to expose the judicial crime. [KN]
keywords: the gold coins and the judge
full_text:
Before embarking on a three-year pilgrimage to Mecca, an honest merchant of Agra named Abdullah sealed one hundred gleaming gold dinars inside a sturdy earthenware jar, covered the gold with pickled olives, and entrusted the jar to the city's chief Qazi (judge) for safekeeping.

'Keep this safe in your cellar, noble Qazi,' Abdullah requested. 'If I do not return, distribute the wealth to orphans.'

Two years passed. One evening, the Qazi's wife craved fresh olives. Remembering the pilgrim's jar, the Qazi opened it. Seeing the plump olives, he spooned some out, only to uncover the glittering gold coins beneath! Greed seized the judge's heart. He dumped all the gold into his private strongbox, threw away the moldering old olives, filled the jar with fresh green olives from the market, and resealed it with wax.

When Abdullah returned to Agra, he thanked the Qazi and retrieved his jar. But upon opening it at home, he found only fresh olives—the gold was gone! He rushed to the Qazi, who shouted: 'Ingrate! You gave me a sealed jar of olives and I returned it untouched! Accuse a holy judge and I will have you whipped!'

Weeping, Abdullah brought his petition to Emperor Akbar, who referred the matter to Birbal.

Birbal examined the jar, the seal, and the olives. He summoned two master olive merchants of Agra and asked: 'Examine these olives. How long have they been preserved in this jar?'

The merchants tasted the fruit and replied: 'Sire, these olives are from the recent autumn harvest, barely two months old! Olives kept in a jar for three years would be black, soft, and sour.'

Birbal turned to the Qazi: 'Abdullah departed three years ago. If this jar remained untouched in your cellar as you swear, how did fresh autumn olives find their way into a three-year-old seal?'

The Qazi began to stammer, claiming Abdullah must have replaced them himself.

Birbal then ordered a brazier brought to the chamber. He carefully scraped a speck of sealing wax from the rim and warmed it, comparing it to the official seal currently resting upon the Qazi's desk. The wax was fresh imperial crimson wax, introduced to Agra only six months earlier, whereas three years ago the court used dark brown lac!

Trapped by forensic proof and the testimony of nature, the Qazi broke down and wept, confessing his theft. Akbar stripped the corrupt judge of his office, restored the gold to Abdullah with interest, and lauded Birbal's meticulous discernment.
